narrationScript: Once you have your webpage's structure defined with HTML, you'll want to make it visually appealing. That's where CSS, or Cascading Style Sheets, comes in. CSS is like the skin and clothing of our webpage body; it dictates the visual presentation—things like colors, fonts, spacing, and overall layout. Without CSS, even a perfectly structured HTML page would appear as plain, unformatted text. A core principle of good web design is separating content, which is HTML, from its presentation, which is CSS. This makes your code cleaner, easier to maintain, and much more flexible. CSS rules are made up of two main parts: a selector and a declaration block. The selector targets the specific HTML element or elements you want to style, for example, `h1` to target all `<h1>` tags. The declaration block then contains one or more declarations, each specifying a property, like `color` or `font-size`, and its corresponding value, such as `navy` or `2em`. So, a rule like `h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2em; }` would select all `<h1>` elements and set their text color to navy and their font size to twice the default.
